wa_mount_christie_west.skip_reason: Approach text stops at establishing a high camp in the Martins Park/Martin Lakes basin on Christie's north side. The broad snow-and-rock couloir leading up toward the peak is only noted as visible from Lower Martins Park; nothing describes climbing it.

climbing_route.label: South Chute
climbing_route.notes: Turn south into the South Chute at the 'Cat Ears' rock landmark. A long, narrowing scree gully climbing about 1,900 ft from the lake to roughly 6,600 ft. Loose underfoot and much better done on residual early-season snow, since bare scree here is notoriously miserable and can sluff rock onto parties below.

climbing_route.label: Saddle and second scree gully to the notch
climbing_route.notes: Above the chute, cross a saddle, drop about 150 ft, and work up a second scree gully to a notch in the summit ridge.

climbing_route.label: Gaps and ledges to the traverse
climbing_route.notes: From the notch the route threads gaps and ledges, marked in places by faded white-paint dots, to the base of the Finger Traverse itself.

climbing_route.label: Finger Traverse
climbing_route.notes: An exposed, downsloping ledge above a large cliff, where climbers jam their fingers into a crack running along the top edge for balance. A rusty, decades-old set of fixed pitons sits along the ledge for parties who want to protect it, though most cross carefully unroped. Figure 5-6+ hours above the lake to the summit.

climbing_route.label: North Chute
climbing_route.notes: Rather than the South Chute used for the Finger Traverse, this route climbs the North Chute higher in the basin — a long, loose gully leading toward the crest. Firm snow, when present, makes the scree/talus below far faster and safer than bare scree.

climbing_route.label: Ledges north to the traverse
climbing_route.notes: Above the chute the route loses a little elevation and traverses north on ledges to reach the base of the Terrible Traverse at about 7,435 ft.

climbing_route.label: Terrible Traverse
climbing_route.notes: A steep, exposed snow (or, late-season, bare rock ledge) crossing directly above a large cliff, where a fall would be unsurvivable. Early-to-mid summer it is a hard, steep snow traverse best done with an ice axe and crampons; by late season it often melts back to a narrow but more secure rock ledge at the base of the icy slope above, which many parties find preferable. Some parties place running protection (pickets in snow) given the consequences of a slip, though it is not a roped rappel move.

climbing_route.label: Broken buttress southwest of Lake Ouzel
climbing_route.notes: From camp, scramble up the large broken buttress southwest of the lake (cairned to aid the return); partway up the buttress traverse far climber's-right, then continue up to gain the Redoubt Glacier easily.

climbing_route.label: Redoubt Glacier to the 8,260-ft notch
climbing_route.notes: Cross/skirt the glacier — crevasse hazard, rope up if conditions warrant — to reach the obvious SW basin near 7,700 ft below Custer's summit, then continue to the 8,260-ft notch immediately south of the true summit.

climbing_route.label: Summit gully (crux)
climbing_route.notes: A short, vertical, 6-8-ft-wide rock gully with occasional ice breaks through the notch; this is the technical crux of the ascent.

climbing_route.label: South Ridge to the summit
climbing_route.notes: Above the gully, follow the loose, chossy South Ridge — widely regarded as some of the worst rock quality in the Cascades, so test every hold — the remaining short distance to the summit.

climbing_route.label: Southeast Ridge crest to the 7600-ft saddle
climbing_route.notes: From the ridge crest around 6800-7000 ft, the route traverses climbers' trail and open scree below the East Summit (7899 ft) — faint where it first leaves the ridge, then well-defined — to a saddle around 7600 ft between the East and Middle Summits. Loose talus and route-finding uncertainty below the East Summit.

climbing_route.label: Final slopes to the West Summit
climbing_route.notes: From the saddle, the final few hundred feet to the true (West) summit (7,960 ft) cross a mix of loose talus, lingering snowfields, and the rocky margin of the Daniel Glacier remnant on the mountain's north side. Carry an ice axe and light crampons even in summer — snow patches can be firm in the morning and steep enough to want them — and the Daniel/Lynch Glacier ice on the north side opens real crevasses by late summer, so stay on the rock/scree spine rather than wandering onto glacier ice.

wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.skip_reason: The text is approach throughout and stops at the base of the southwest line. Everything above camp — the Stump Hollow traverse, the 6400 ft saddle, the descent into Crescent Creek Basin, the Barrier crossing, and the snowfield/small glacier below Degenhardt's south side — is described as the approach to the base; no climbing above it is described.

climbing_route.label: Broad bench and scree slope east of the summit
climbing_route.notes: From camp in Ferry Basin (~5,700 ft), the summit is reached via a broad bench and scree/talus slope east of the true summit, described in trip reports as loose 'dagger scree' (sharp, shifting shale-like rock) that demands careful footing but involves no technical climbing, just sustained off-trail scrambling. Expect lingering snow/ice in gullies and on north-facing slopes even in August (ice axe and often crampons are standard kit) and serious route-finding responsibility.

climbing_route.label: Mazama Dome-Herman connecting ridge crest
climbing_route.notes: Once on the ridge, follow its crest generally eastward, staying mostly on the south/southwest side over heather benches and loose scree/talus, to the base of a short final east ridge.

climbing_route.label: Final east ridge
climbing_route.notes: The short final east ridge leads to the true summit at 6,285 ft.
